newsitem.title: UK: Adams non-committal on N.Irish truce prospects.
newsitem.headline: Adams non-committal on N.Irish truce prospects.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, refused on Thursday to speculate whether his guerrilla allies would call a truce after the Protestant Orange Order bowed to Roman Catholic anger and called off weekend parades.
"I am not going to speculate about the IRA (Irish Republican Army)...I cannot speculate about how the IRA will respond to these developments," Adams told a news conference.

He was responding to speculation that the IRA might match an unprecedented concession by the Orange Order, its ideological opposites, and call a ceasefire to its 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland.

The Orange Order, which wants the province to remain British, unexpectedly called off, or re-routed, four parades late on Thursday night that minority Irish Catholics had threatened to challenge with mass counter demonstrations.

"A door has been opened which raises the possibility of a durable resolution to this (marching) issue," Adams said. "This will be problematic but let us leave no stone unturned in our efforts to achieve."
The province has been gripped by a fear of inter-communal violence since Sunday when Britain allowed 1200 "Orangemen" to parade through a Catholic enclave in the town of Portadown.
The move triggered days of Catholic rioting and IRA shooting attacks and cast relations between London and the 40 percent Catholic population to their lowest level for more than a year.
People in both communities said that the Orders' olive branch had brought the province back from the brink of disaster.
It raised hopes that the IRA, which draws support from Catholics, would reciprocate by calling off its war to win Sinn Fein a seat at Anglo-Irish peace talks.
Mo Mowlam, Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, told breakfast radio as the province digested news of the Order's U-turn decision, "I hope the IRA call a new ceasefire."
She said Sinn Fein could, under Britain's latest conditions, join the talks within six weeks if the IRA's truce was deemed credible. "The ball is in their court", she told the BBC.

Adams, who says that Sinn Fein does not speak for the guerrillas, said he had been told that many planned street "mobilisations" by Catholic protestors, planned for, July 12, the Order's biggest marching day, had been cancelled.

It was not initially clear, however, if Catholics would go ahead with protests at three small parades which have sparked friction in previous years in the rural villages of Dunloy, Bellaghy and Newtownbutler.
"I welcome and acknowledge the significance of the decisions taken by the Orange Order last night. They have created a welcome breathing space...," Adams said.

"There remains the problem of a number of scheduled contentious parades during this marching season'... I would urge the local Orange lodges (organisers) in these areas to immediately enter into talks with local residents."

Britain says that the IRA, which killed two police officers in the town of Lurgan last month, must abandon violence before Sinn Fein is admitted to talks. The Irish and American governments are of the same mind.

Sinn Fein argues that a 17 per cent vote in Britain's May 1 elections gives it an automatic right to be at the negotiating table but Protestant parties say they will not sit down with a group which has a private army in the wings.
